US midterms: Key US figure during Galwan crisis, Eileen Laubacher beats Trump ally for House seat
She will represent Colorado’s 4th district, which was thought to be safely Republican, given that it backed Trump comfortably in the 2024 presidential election.
Former US Navy rear admiral and veteran India expert Eileen Laubacher defeated Lauren Boebert, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, to win election to the US House of Representatives, CNN projected on Monday.
A member of the Democratic party, Laubacher edged out Boebert by just over 3,000 votes in a major upset victory that took nearly a week to confirm. She will represent Colorado’s 4th district, which was thought to be safely Republican, given that it backed Trump comfortably in the 2024 presidential election.
Prior to announcing her run for Congress, Laubacher held a series of high-level national security jobs that made her a crucial figure in the US-India relationship. She served as a military attache and senior defence official at the US Embassy in New Delhi, after which she returned to Washington for the crucial role of Senior Director for South Asia at the White House-based National Security Council (NSC).
Also read | Indian-Americans Ranjeev Puri, Priya Sundareshan elected to head Michigan, Arizona legislatures
Laubacher is well known in both the US and Indian national security establishments for her key role during the 2020 Galwan crisis between India and China. At the height of the border crisis, she facilitated the supply of cold weather clothing to Indian troops and the sharing of crucial military intelligence with New Delhi.
“During the Galwan crisis, whether it was imagery, cold weather gear or other assets, we provided what India needed in record time. As the US Senior Defence Official in New Delhi, Eileen played a crucial and indispensable role in that process,” said Basant Sanghera, a State Department and NSC veteran who is now managing principal at the Asia Group, a geopolitical consultancy.
Other former colleagues said Laubacher is also known for her ability to build a rapport with Indian policymakers and military officials. Her elevation to the position of senior director for South Asia at the National Security Council in 2022 was seen as unusual, as the role has generally gone to political appointees. Her appointment as a serving military officer was seen as a reflection of her abilities, former colleagues told HT.
Also read | Seats with largest Indian-American populations in US mostly went blue
During her time in Washington, Laubacher was credited with steering a major agreement with New Delhi to co-develop F414 engines for India’s Tejas Mk2 fighter jet. Her colleagues also credited her skill at managing bureaucratic differences within the US government to drive key priorities with India, like the Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET). People familiar with the details told HT that she played a key role in stabilising the US-India partnership in 2023 and 2024 after accusations surfaced that an Indian government official had directed a plot to assassinate noted pro-Khalistan separatist Gurpatwant Pannun.
Laubacher’s election to the House of Representatives will bolster the ranks of legislators with India experience, especially after the departure of several veteran lawmakers in January next year.
Congressmen Raja Krishnamoorthi, Shri Thanedar, Bill Huizenga and Brian Fitzpatrick – all key supporters of the US-India relationship – will leave the House in January. They will be joined by Texas Senator John Cornyn, who was seen as a reliable backer of the bilateral partnership in the upper chamber.
Also read | 84/100: Democrats sweep districts with high concentration of Indian-American voters in midterms
“I think her election will be a very welcome development for the relationship. Having a person who can be a catalyst for driving US-India ties forward from Capitol Hill – both in terms of future cooperation and ability to provide guidance when the relationship hits a rough spot – will be important,” said Sanghera.
Her Republican rival Boebert is one of the most recognisable figures in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, known for her combative style and a string of controversies.
A graduate of the US Naval Academy, Laubacher was commissioned into the navy in 1990 and was promoted to the rank of rear admiral in 2018. In this, she followed her father, Vice Admiral Michael Haskins, who served as commander of US naval forces in Japan during the 1990s. She served in Bermuda, the United Kingdom and Afghanistan prior to her posting in India.

Critics of Republican Representative Lauren Boebert took to social media to celebrate as one early projection showed the polarizing conservative lawmaker losing her bid for a fourth term in Congress.
The projection from CNN -- no other outlet has made the call -- indicates that Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy Rear Admiral who served over three decades in military service, will flip Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.
With an estimated 98 percent of the vote counted, CNN reported Laubacher holding 48.8 percent, or 185,923 votes, to Boebert’s 47.9 percent, or 182,686 votes. Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris drew 3.3 percent, or 12,605 votes.
Following the projection, opponents of the MAGA firebrand congresswoman quickly weighed in online. Many posts referenced Boebert’s 2023 removal from a Denver theater during a performance of the musical “Beetlejuice.” The congresswoman was escorted out of the Denver venue after vaping, singing, taking flash photos and groping her date — an incident she initially denied until security camera footage was released, prompting a public apology tour.
Laubacher also weighed in on the CNN projection, releasing a statement on social media that she is grateful for all the support that led to victory and ready to get to work for the people of Colorado. “We made history. Now let’s make a difference,” she said in part.
Boebert denied the claims in a video posted to X hours later.
“Just a quick reminder that counties still have until November 13th under Colorado law to finish counting and curing every eligible ballot,” she says. “Declaring victory now is like icing a cake before it comes out of the oven.”
Author Don Winslow reacted to the early call on X, writing, “LAUREN BOEBERT HAS LOST! TODAY IS A GREAT DAY.”
Progressive commentator Isaiah Martin posted, “LAUREN BOEBERT, YOU'RE FIRED!!!!!!”
The tight contest follows a strategic gamble by the 39-year-old congresswoman, who opted to switch from Colorado’s 3rd District to the more reliably Republican 4th District last cycle to safeguard her seat. The move came after a razor-thin 2022 victory over Democrat Adam Frisch by just 546 votes, though she later secured reelection in 2024 by more than 11 points.
Political commentator Adam Mockler pointed to her shift between districts, posting on X, “The best part is, Lauren Boebert moved to a ‘safer’ district and still lost.”
Throughout her time in the House of Representatives, Boebert established herself as a central figure in the party’s MAGA wing, frequently drawing national attention and internal party tension.
Former President Joe Biden once singled her out as “one of the leaders of this extreme MAGA movement” following her heckling during his 2022 State of the Union address, and her vocal stance frequently presented management challenges for Republican Speakers Kevin McCarthy and Mike Johnson.
Her relationship with Donald Trump also experienced turbulent moments despite his late endorsement praising her as a “MAGA Warrior.”
Trump briefly targeted her earlier in the year after she campaigned with Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie, calling her “dumb” and “weak-minded” while threatening to pull his support.
Boebert further broke rank with House GOP leadership and the Trump administration when she backed a Democratic effort to release Jeffrey Epstein case files, defying party leaders who cited privacy concerns for victims.
Laubacher’s campaign focused heavily on local economic and affordability issues while capitalizing on broader national headwinds facing the Republican Party.

Lauren Boebert Faces Election Defeat as Democrat Eileen Laubacher Leads in Trump-Won Colorado District
CNN's projection follows a narrow lead for the retired Navy rear admiral, but counting and certification are still pending
Republican Representative Lauren Boebert is facing an election setback as Democrat Eileen Laubacher takes the lead in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, a traditionally Republican stronghold that also backed President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
CNN's Decision Desk projected Laubacher to win on Monday, 9 November 2026. The result would end Boebert's congressional tenure after three terms and mark a significant shift in the district's political representation.
According to Associated Press figures reported by 9NEWS, Laubacher had received 185,923 votes against Boebert's 182,686, giving her a lead of 3,237 votes. Approximately 97.9% of the estimated ballots had been counted as of 10 November, although the results remained unofficial pending the completion of the counting and certification process.
Laubacher's Military and Government Background
Laubacher is a retired US Navy rear admiral who served for 34 years, building a career in military leadership, international security and diplomacy. According to her official Navy biography, she deployed to Afghanistan in 2009 and later served as Senior Defence Official and Defence Attaché to India from June 2019 to June 2022.
In that role, she represented US defence interests in India and worked on military and security cooperation between the two countries. She subsequently joined the National Security Council as Senior Director for South Asia, serving from October 2022 to May 2024. She retired from the Navy in October 2024.
Laubacher drew on this experience during her congressional campaign, presenting her record in military and government service as a key qualification for public office. She also emphasised affordability and leadership, addressing concerns she said were important to voters in Colorado's 4th Congressional District.
Boebert's Political Career Faces Setback
Boebert was first elected to Congress in 2020 after defeating Republican incumbent Scott Tipton in Colorado's 3rd Congressional District primary. She moved to the 4th District ahead of the 2024 election and won against Democrat Trisha Calvarese with 53.6% of the vote.
CNN described Boebert as one of the House Republican conference's most recognisable conservative figures and a prominent Trump ally.
Their relationship, however, became strained. In May 2026, Trump criticised Boebert after she supported Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican who had opposed the president on key issues. Trump called her 'dumb' and 'weak-minded' and threatened to withdraw his endorsement.
He later backed her re-election campaign, describing her as a 'MAGA Warrior'.
Recount Remains a Possibility
According to Colorado's election calendar, counties must complete ballot tabulation by 13 November, while the county canvass and submission of official results are scheduled to conclude by 25 November.
Under Colorado law, an automatic recount is required when the margin between the leading candidates is no more than 0.5% of the winner's vote total. Based on the reported figures, Laubacher's 3,237-vote lead represents approximately 1.74% of her total, placing the current margin outside the automatic recount threshold.
However, a candidate or interested party may request a recount at their own expense, subject to state requirements.
Boebert's campaign said it was investigating what it described as 'unusual voting patterns'. Its attorney, Scott Gessler, raised concerns but did not publicly provide details supporting the allegations, according to USA TODAY.
CNN's projection has put Laubacher in a strong position, but the result remains subject to the completion of the official counting and certification process. If confirmed, her victory would end Boebert's congressional tenure and flip a heavily Republican Colorado seat to the Democrats.

sources.news_title: Democrat Eileen Laubacher declares victory over Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District
sources.text:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher declared victory Monday in her race against U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a polarizing crusader for the Make America Great Again movement whose apparent defeat in Colorado’s most conservative district is the latest fallout of the blue wave that crashed over President Donald Trump’s coalition last week.
While the Associated Press had not yet called the 4th Congressional District race Monday afternoon and Boebert has not conceded, CNN projected Laubacher would win the tight contest.
Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, continued to slightly expand her lead with new vote totals Monday evening, maintaining her 48.8%-to-47.9% split with Boebert — a margin of just under 1 percentage point, but not close enough to trigger an automatic recount.
Only a smattering of ballots remained to be processed in several counties, including military and overseas votes. More than 98% of votes in the 4th District have been counted, the AP estimated.
“The way we won this race is the way I intend to continue serving the people, which is going everywhere, talking a little bit and listening a lot,” Laubacher said in an interview with The Denver Post on Monday afternoon. “It’s up to me to now deliver for people and make the changes that are going to improve their lives.”
Boebert’s campaign staff did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Post. But the incumbent shared a video on social media Monday evening in which she said “CNN and the Democrats” had called the race prematurely, with votes still left to be counted or “cured” of signature discrepancies by Friday’s deadline.
“Declaring victory now is like icing a cake before it comes out of the oven,” Boebert said in the video address to her supporters. “…Regardless of the final outcome, we will move forward to future victories together. We’ll make sure every eligible vote is counted and that every single voice is heard before we take any next steps.”
She did not repeat the vague claims of possible voting irregularities made by a campaign attorney last week.
Laubacher, a former Republican who only recently became a Democrat, moved to Highlands Ranch with her husband two years ago. She doesn’t align with the more radical wing of her new party, and did not endorse Melat Kiros, the democratic socialist who beat U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette in the 1st Congressional District primary and won the seat on Election Day.
“I’m a very moderate person,” Laubacher told The Post in October. “I’ve never been a straight-party ticket voter — I’ve never felt either party matched me perfectly.”
In an interview Monday, Laubacher said she would work with anyone regardless of party to pass “meaningful legislation” such as rolling back Trump’s tariffs, ending the war in Iran and “cracking down on corruption.”
“I’m encouraged by the idea that we can work across the aisle to get things done for the American people. It is what we have to do,” she said.
Laubacher was in Washington, D.C., on Monday to participate in new member orientation even as the remaining votes continue to be counted.
While the vast majority of the members in attendance will have already won their races, it isn’t uncommon for someone whose race is still in limbo to attend. In 2022, Adam Frisch, another Democratic opponent of Boebert’s, went to the Capitol for the orientation. He was more than 1,000 votes behind Boebert at the time in a race to represent Colorado’s 3rd Congressional District, and ultimately lost the election.
Boebert and Trump’s pre-election clash
Boebert had fallen out of favor with the president after she was one of four Republicans to vote last year to force the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files. She also helped campaign in Kentucky for Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, a foe of Trump’s who ultimately lost his primary, and spoke out against the president’s veto of a bill to fund clean drinking water for Colorado.
Trump posted on Truth Social in May asking for people to run against Boebert, calling her “weak-minded” and a “carpetbagger” for switching to the 4th Congressional District. Three days before the election, though, Trump endorsed Boebert, calling her “a MAGA Warrior.”
Laubacher significantly outraised Boebert in the race. In late October, the Cook Political Report recategorized the district from “solid Republican” to “leans Republican.”
Voters in the 4th District, which is currently the most Republican-leaning of Colorado’s eight congressional districts, have put a Democrat in the seat only once in the last 53 years. And it was for just one term.
Two years ago, Boebert moved to Windsor in the 4th District after nearly losing the seat she held for two terms in the Western Slope’s 3rd Congressional District. Voters in the 4th District, which spans the state’s Eastern Plains and parts of metro Denver, leaned 27 percentage points in favor of Republicans earlier this decade, according to nonpartisan redistricting staffers.
The 4th District race was one of three close Colorado congressional contests for Republican incumbents in the fallout of the massive blue wave that swept across the country Tuesday. U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, the state’s fourth Republican incumbent member of Congress, lost his race in the 8th Congressional District to Democrat Manny Rutinel on election night.
On Thursday, the Associated Press called the Colorado Springs-based 5th Congressional District for Jessica Killin, the Democratic challenger to freshman Rep. Jeff Crank. It’s the first time that district has ever had a Democratic representative.
And the wire service on Friday declared Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd the winner of the 3rd Congressional District.
In Boebert’s race, the results show that Laubacher carried the more urban — and more populous — corners of the district, including Douglas and Arapahoe counties, while Boebert led in most rural counties, including Weld.
As of Monday evening, the 3,352-vote margin was well outside the threshold for an automatic recount, currently 931 votes (0.5% of the race leader’s vote total).
Scott Gessler, an attorney for Boebert’s campaign, said in a statement to media last week that the campaign was “fighting for every vote.” He said, without citing specifics, that the campaign was “investigating some very unusual voting patterns and expect this election to head to a recount, one way or another.”
In Colorado, candidates can choose to pay for recounts regardless of the margin of their loss.
Officials will continue counting the remaining ballots, which include votes from military members and people overseas, until Friday. Voters whose ballots were rejected because of signature discrepancies can also “cure” their ballots by that time.
“This is standard practice in every election,” said Jack Todd, a spokesman for the Colorado Secretary of State’s Office.
From Shooters Grill to Congress
In 2019, Boebert, then in her early 30s, seemed to come out of nowhere to take on the Herculean task of unseating longtime Republican incumbent Scott Tipton in the 3rd District, which covers most of western Colorado and wraps around Pueblo to the south.
A one-time owner of the now-defunct restaurant Shooters Grill in Rifle, where staff carried guns, Boebert drove across the state to attend a Beto O’Rourke presidential rally in Aurora. Openly carrying a gun and standing in a sea of Democrats, she challenged the candidate’s position on gun safety.
She not only beat Tipton in the GOP primary the following year, but she also went on to win the general election, becoming the first woman to hold the seat.
In her time in Congress, Boebert has been known for bombastic statements that frequently drew national attention. She largely remained defiant in the face of criticism, but was unable to ride out the controversy she created in September 2023 when she was booted from a performance of “Beetlejuice” at Denver’s Buell Theatre after fellow patrons complained about her openly vaping, making out with her date and filming the show against house rules.
After that story went global, she apologized for her behavior but quickly came to realize her standing had fallen so far with her 3rd District constituents that she decamped for friendlier environs — and a more conservative — district on the Eastern Plains.
Her move turned out to be prescient. After battling it out against five GOP challengers in the June 2024 primary for the 4th District, Boebert cruised to victory that November.
While Boebert often made headlines for the wrong reasons, she also delivered for her constituents. Over her two terms in the 3rd District, she helped shepherd the bipartisan Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basins Endangered Fish Recovery Programs Reauthorization Act into law, extending protection for four threatened and endangered native fish species.
Then-President Joe Biden also signed the CONVEY Act, a Boebert-led bill that directs the Bureau of Land Management to sell to Mesa County a 31-acre parcel in Clifton for economic development.
After Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, Boebert became a reliable ally for the president. She largely supported his agenda, but cracks soon appeared in the relationship — most notably in her push to have the Epstein files released, something Trump initially resisted.
She also gave a biting assessment of the president’s decision in the waning days of 2025 to veto a bipartisan rural water bill that would have funded a pipeline to bring clean water to 50,000 residents in southeast Colorado.
She told 9News at the time that she hoped the president’s “veto has nothing to do with political retaliation for calling out corruption and demanding accountability. Americans deserve leadership that puts people over politics.”
The libertarian candidate
Then there’s the candidate in the 4th District race that no one is talking about.
Doug Mangeris is a 39-year-old commercial construction superintendent from Loveland who ran as a Libertarian. He garnered more than 12,600 votes, a number well above the 3,352 votes currently separating Boebert and Laubacher.
Mangeris’ vote total brings back echoes of 2022, when in the eyes of many political watchers in Colorado, a Libertarian candidate in the ultra-competitive 8th Congressional District contest cost the race for Republican state Sen. Barb Kirkmeyer.
With 9,280 votes, a tattooed, punk-music-loving electrician named Richard Ward drew enough support that, had those votes gone largely to Kirkmeyer, they would have cost Democrat Yadira Caraveo the close election.
Like Ward four years ago, Mangeris said he put few resources into his campaign for the 4th.
“I didn’t send any mailers, I didn’t knock on any doors, I didn’t stand on any street corners,” he said. “I didn’t have the money that would have allowed me not to work and instead run a campaign.”
He prefers Boebert to Laubacher, but said neither major party is doing much good for the country.
“It’s foreign interests; it’s not the interests of the constituents,” Mangeris said. “Our country is headed in a bad way, especially with all the socialists that just got elected.”
Lori Korman was Mangeris’ campaign treasurer. She also happens to be his mother. A mail carrier in Loveland for the past decade, she said what struck her in the weeks leading up to Election Day was the utter absence of any mailings or flyers from Boebert’s campaign.
“I never saw any campaigning from her,” Korman said. That extended to campaign yard signs on her route. “If she had tried harder, she would have gotten more votes.”
Boebert, Mangeris said, took it for granted that she wouldn’t lose such a reliably Republican district.
“I ran just as much, if not more, of a race as Boebert did,” he said.

WASHINGTON — Republican Representative Lauren Boebert has lost her bid for a fourth term in Congress, according to a projection by CNN on Monday, after Democrat Eileen Laubacher overcame the district’s longstanding conservative advantage in a major political upset.
Laubacher, a retired Navy two-star rear admiral and former national security official, defeated Boebert in a closely fought contest that remained uncalled for nearly a week following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The outcome marks a dramatic shift in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District — a reliable Republican stronghold stretching across the state’s Eastern Plains into the Denver suburbs — and adds another seat to the incoming Democratic House majority.

No, we’re simply here to help with a list of shows custom-picked for you following your exit. Below, check out a few productions we think you might enjoy after your ejection from public office. Who Is Eileen Laubacher?
Laubacher served 34 years in the Navy, including as the senior U.S. defense official and defense attaché in India, before joining the Biden administration as the National Security Council’s senior director for South Asia.
When Was Lauren Boebert First Elected?
Prior to entering politics Boebert ran and owned Shooters Grill, a restaurant in Rifle, Colorado, where staff members were permitted to openly carry firearms.
She was first elected to the House representing Colorado’s 3rd Congressional District in November 2020, swiftly acquired a reputation as one of President Donald Trump’s most outspoken supporters in the lower chamber of Congress.
She attracted national attention for incidents including heckling President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and was a vocal supporter of Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.
In 2024, Boebert was elected to a third term after switching to Colorado’s Republican-leaning 4th Congressional District, beating Democrat Trisha Calvarese, 53.6 percent to 42.4 percent.
In November 2025, Boebert was one of four House Republicans who defied the White House and signed a discharge petition to force a vote on releasing the Department of Justice’s files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The petition helped force congressional action that culminated in the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which Trump signed into law on November 19, 2025.
In May 2026, Trump suggested that Boebert should face a Republican primary challenge after she campaigned for Kentucky GOP Representative Thomas Massie, who had clashed with the president over his One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the Epstein files. Massie was defeated in the primary by Trump-backed Ed Gallrein.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote: “Boebert is campaigning for the Worst ’Republican’ Congressman in the History of our Country, Thomas Massie, of the Great Commonwealth of Kentucky, and anybody who can be that dumb deserves a good Primary fight.”
Boebert responded on X: “Yes, I saw the President’s post. No, I’m not mad or offended. I knew the risks when I agreed to stand by my friend Thomas Massie. I was, and will be, America First, America Always, and MAGA.”
Controversies
In September 2023, Boebert and a male companion were escorted out of a performance of Beetlejuice: The Musical in Denver for causing a disturbance, with surveillance footage appearing to show the pair touching each other intimately, while Boebert later acknowledged that she had been vaping.
Boebert apologized for the incident that she said “fell short of my values,” adding that it had been a “challenging personal time for me and my entire family” due to her ongoing divorce.
In 2024, Boebert was briefly investigated by police after her ex-husband, Jayson Boebert, accused her of punching him in a Colorado restaurant. She denied the allegation and was not charged. Police closed the investigation, saying there was a lack of evidence.

In his endorsement, Trump called Boebert an “America First Patriot” and a “MAGA Warrior” who was “doing an incredible job representing Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.” He added: “Lauren Boebert has my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election. GET OUT AND VOTE FOR LAUREN — SHE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”
Why Haven't Alaska, Mississippi Senate Races Been Called?
The Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remain uncalled nearly a week after Election Day.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,500 votes, with mail and affidavit ballots still being processed and voters having until November 10 to resolve certain identification issues.
Alaska has an even longer counting process because of its ranked-choice voting system. Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan as officials continue processing ballots from across the vast state.

Democrat Laubacher declares victory against Republican Rep. Boebert in Colorado’s 4th District
Conservative district that covers Eastern Plains flips as part of ‘blue tsunami’
Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert, left, and Democrat Eileen Laubacher appear at a debate hosted by 9News on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)
Democrat Eileen Laubacher declared victory Monday over Republican U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert in the race to represent Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.
The Associated Press had yet to call the race Monday, when Laubacher had 48.8% of the vote over Boebert’s 47.9%. Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris had 3.3% of the vote. The AP estimated 98% of votes in the race were counted at the time.
“Over 17 months, I traveled 40,000 miles across all 21 counties. The message was clear: Coloradans are tired of political games, broken promises, and being ignored by Washington,” Laubacher said in a statement. “They want someone who will fight for them and deliver results.”
Laubacher attended orientation for new members of Congress Monday.
Scott Gessler, an attorney for Boebert’s campaign who represented President Donald Trump during a lawsuit that sought to remove him from the ballot in 2024, said in a statement last week that the campaign will fight to ensure every “legal vote” is counted, and it was “investigating some very unusual voting patterns.” Boebert voted against certifying results from the 2020 election, which former President Joe Biden won.
Boebert’s campaign did not immediately respond to Newsline’s request for comment.
The 4th District, which includes most of Douglas County and the Eastern Plains, has in recent years been considered Colorado’s most conservative district. While the district was previously considered safely Republican, some analyses of the Boebert-Laubacher race recently put the district in the “leans Republican” category.
National Democrats looking to flip the district named it a top priority this election. The last Democrat to represent the district was former U.S. Rep. Betsy Markey, who was elected in 2008. She served one term.
Laubacher, a first-time candidate, is a retired Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official. She was a longtime Republican but switched her party affiliation, first to unaffiliated, and then to Democratic in 2024. She defended that action at a debate against Boebert by saying her belief in personal liberties is currently found in the Democratic Party and that the GOP she historically supported is “nearly unrecognizable.”
Boebert, of Windsor, was first elected to represent the 3rd District on the Western Slope, but she moved across the state after two terms when she nearly lost reelection in 2022. She is a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, but a rift arose earlier this year when Boebert campaigned alongside outgoing Kentucky U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, whom the president targeted for leading efforts to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files last year.
Two other congressional seats in Colorado previously held by Republicans flipped to Democrats in last week’s election as part of a “blue tsunami” that swept the state and the country. Republican Rep. Gabe Evans lost his race to Democrat Manny Rutinel in the 8th District, and Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost his race to Democrat Jessica Killin in the 5th District. With Boebert’s loss, the state’s congressional delegation will favor Democrats 7-1.

Colorado MAGA Representative Lauren Boebert has been washed away in the blue wave, losing her election to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a stunning upset that is one of many GOP midterm failures.

In 2023, Boebert and a male partner were kicked out of a showing of Beetlejuice for vaping, singing, filming, and groping one another. Outgoing Representative Andy Ogles was under investigation for alleged campaign finance law violations.
Representative Andy Ogles
Heather Diehl/Getty Images
Representative Andy Ogles
Representative Andy Ogles’s legal team pleaded with the Trump administration to drop a probe into his campaign finances. Months later, the Justice Department complied.
Emails obtained by the nonprofit organization American Oversight and published Monday by RawStory revealed that Ogles’s attorneys reached out to the then-director of the DOJ’s Weaponization Working Group, Edward Martin, to end the investigation in November 2025.
“Please see the attached letter on behalf of our client, Rep. Andy Ogles, seeking the termination of the Department’s criminal investigation into campaign finance issues that are more appropriately addressed by the FEC and the House Ethics Committee,” the email read.
Two weeks later, after no response from Martin, Ogles’s legal team followed up to prompt a written response, this time cc-ing Jordan Fox, the chief of staff to then-deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“Received. Thank you,” Martin responded, signing off as “Ed.”
Months later in May, the DOJ agreed to return Ogles’s cell phone back to the Tennessee lawmaker, signalling the end of the inquiry.
It is not clear if Martin followed through on escalating Ogles’s request to DOJ higher ups, or if the request was immediately tied to the end result. But it is an alarming indication of how backdoor favors are clearly expected, and how they operate, within the Trump administration, particularly for the president’s most loyal MAGA lapdogs.
The investigation was related to discrepancies in Ogles’s 2022 campaign finance records, when he filed a report claiming that he loaned his campaign $320,000. The detail raised alarm bells in 2024, when Ogles filed another campaign finance report to acknowledge that he had only loaned the campaign $20,000.

The lawmaker’s legal defense torched the FBI’s decision to claim his phone, arguing that the bureau—as a component of the executive branch—had no right to look at the personal communications of a sitting member of the legislative branch.

Representative Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment accuse the defense secretary of “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

Representative Thomas Massie presented eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Monday afternoon.
Massie posted his draft resolution hours earlier on X with the message, “I’ve seen some of my colleagues say @SecWar Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they’ll vote not to impeach. They’ll have hearings & trials.”
Massie said last Wednesday that Hegseth could avert the vote if he resigned. That may be Hegseth’s plan, as he has called a press conference at the Pentagon Tuesday. Have Senate Democrats found a challenger to Schumer?
Senator Chuck Schumer and Senator Chris Van Hollen
Drew Angerer/Getty Images
Senator Chuck Schumer and Senator Chris Van Hollen
Senator Chris Van Hollen is open to running for Senate majority leader, amid mounting calls for Senator Chuck Schumer to pass the torch.
Van Hollen has “received an outpouring of calls and is now in active listening mode,” a person familiar with the Maryland Democrat’s thinking told Politico’s Playbook Monday.
“The door is not shut,” the person added.
Speaking to Fox 5 last week, Van Hollen indicated that he was interested in pursuing a higher office—but not the one people are begging him to take. “I’ve made clear that I’m not looking to be the next Democratic leader,” Van Hollen said. “I’ve been kicking the tires on a 2028 presidential election.”
But the Marylander declined to commit his support to Schumer, who has led the Democrats in the Senate since 2017.
“I think it’s important that the Senate Democratic Caucus have a full and open debate before we select the next leader, whoever that may be. I don’t think it should be automatic. And I think we need to have a plan, and we need to make it clear we’re going to be united by a common plan,” Van Hollen said.
He doubled down on his comments over the weekend, arguing that “nobody should get a blank check” without a greater discussion in the Democratic caucus.
Van Hollen has emerged as a leading progressive, after he traveled to El Salvador when his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García was illegally deported to a foreign gulag.
Van Hollen wasn’t the only Democratic senator who held back on supporting Schumer: Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut also declined to endorse the longtime caucus leader.
At the same time, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has publicly endorsed Van Hollen for the top post. “If he decides he wants to be Senate majority leader, I think he’d be amazing at the job,” El-Sayed told CNN last week.
Pete Hegseth’s Future Looks Grim as Even Trump Starts to Turn on Him
The defense secretary could face an impeachment vote in the House as soon as this week.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appears to be on the verge of getting kicked out of Washington.
Capitol Hill Republicans—including the president—have started to turn on Hegseth publicly. The bombastic former Fox News host could face a House impeachment vote as early as this week.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie originally introduced a 34-page impeachment resolution against the Defense secretary in mid-September, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors, and specifically of abusing the power of his office by advancing Donald Trump’s war against Iran without congressional approval.
Texas Senator Ted Cruz suggested that “one of the reasons the House has been out of session for a couple months is because they didn’t have the votes to stop a Hegseth impeachment” when Massie originally announced the articles. That has not changed.
Massie told MS NOW Monday that he planned to force a vote on the impeachment resolution that afternoon. Several members of the GOP believe it will pass.
But some conservatives are mulling over other solutions that could similarly strip Hegseth of his authority. Speaking with CNN’s Manu Raju Monday morning, retiring Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said it would be easier if Hegseth just resigned.
“I’m weighing it,” Bacon said when asked about the proposed articles of impeachment. “Eight articles, and I’m not very sympathetic to those articles.”
“But the areas that concern me most about the secretary aren’t in the articles of impeachment: firing and redlining abiding generals or admirals; withholding appropriated money all year from Ukraine,” Bacon said. “I’m not the only one that feels this way, there’s a bunch of us that have been talking about it.”
“Some of us don’t feel comfortable with [Massie’s] justifications,” Bacon added, describing Massie’s approach as libertarian, “but I think there are other ones out there.”
Even Trump blamed Hegseth for the Iran war, one of the main reasons Republicans lost so badly last week, while speaking to Fox News from West Palm Beach, Florida on Sunday. Trump claimed that the Pentagon chief was “one of the guys that was most responsible” for the conflict.
Exactly what becomes of the bombastic “secretary of war”—or his political future—after such an ousting is unclear.
Last week, Trump mused about the possibility of effectively pushing Hegseth into Tennessee’s open Senate seat. Trump told reporters Hegseth would be “very popular” as a replacement for Governor-elect Marsha Blackburn. The Hill reported that Hegseth had shown interest in the job, and was actively campaigning for it behind the scenes.
But that’s unlikely to happen: A source close to Blackburn told the Associated Press Thursday that Hegseth was not in consideration for the seat, and dismissed the ongoing rumors as “baseless chatter.”

sources.news_title: Lauren Boebert Loses Colorado House Seat, CNN Projects
sources.text:
Lauren Boebert has lost her seat in Congress to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, CNN projected Monday, closing out one of the biggest upsets of the midterms in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, the most Republican district in the state.
Laubacher, 58, is a retired Navy rear admiral who served more than three decades and later worked on the National Security Council. With about 98% of the vote counted, she led 48.8% to 47.9%, a margin of 3,237 votes, according to CNN. Libertarian Douglas Mangeris took about 3.3%. The Associated Press had not called the race as of Monday afternoon.
On paper, this seat was never supposed to be in play. The Republican who held it before Lauren Boebert routinely won by more than 20 points, and Boebert carried it by about 11 points two years ago. In the final week before Election Day, national forecasters moved the race to “leans Republican,” one step away from a tossup.
The political news that affects your wallet, your rights and your vote, broken down in plain language. Free in your inbox.
Boebert only landed in this district because she left a close fight. In 2022, she held onto her old Western Slope seat by fewer than 600 votes, then switched to the 4th District, which covers the Eastern Plains, Douglas County and the Loveland area, and called it a fresh start. Trump endorsed her again in the days before the election.
Laubacher ran on affordability and buried Boebert in fundraising, pulling in nearly $14 million to Boebert’s roughly $1.2 million.
The count swung for days. At one point Thursday, Laubacher’s lead shrank from 2.2% to 0.65% before growing again. Once Weld County, Boebert’s strongest county, finished counting, the remaining ballots came largely from Arapahoe, Douglas and Larimer counties, where Laubacher was winning.
Lauren Boebert is not conceding. Her campaign attorney, former Colorado Secretary of State Scott Gessler, said the campaign is “investigating some very unusual voting patterns” and expects the race to head to a recount “one way or another.” He did not say what those patterns were, and the campaign has not formally requested a recount.
A recount is not automatic here. Colorado only pays for a recount when the gap between the top two candidates is 0.5% or less of the leading candidate’s vote total. In this race, that works out to about 921 votes, and Laubacher’s lead is more than three times that. Boebert can still request one, but her campaign would have to pay for it, and it would have to be finished by December 8.
Boebert also got the rule wrong in a fundraising email, telling supporters the race would go to an automatic recount if the margin was 0.5% or lower. As Colorado Politics pointed out, the threshold is 0.5% of the leading candidate’s votes, which is a much smaller number than half a percentage point.
Paid recounts in Colorado have rarely changed much. In 2022, Tina Peters paid for a recount after losing the Republican primary for secretary of state, and both candidates picked up 13 votes, leaving the result exactly where it was.
